sections.title: What a schedule is, and where its timer lives
sections.intro: Design: docs/plans/schedule-system.md. A schedule is a fn to run + a dayspan schedule (Oryoli's stored ScheduleInput) + a time zone + args as a gin program run at each firing. The types in the doc are written against the recommended answers; nothing is built until you approve them.

questions.question: Is a schedule a fn of a kind (`schedule/schedule`, a saved fn like a code fn or a widget), or a record the schedule system keeps?
questions.why: It decides where schedules are stored, versioned, shared and searched, and whether firing the target needs a new grant.

options.label: A fn kind
options.description: Your word 'payload' fits: the hub stores, versions, shares and searches schedules, the fn page shows them, describe gives the target as its dep (so calling it needs no new grant), and calling the schedule by name is 'run now'. Firings are records (`schedule/Firing`), since missed and skipped ones have no run.

options.label: Records
options.description: A `schedule/Schedule` record per schedule (person-owned, as Claude sessions are). Simpler for the hub, but no fn page or versions-as-fns, and firing the target needs its own grant rule.

options.label: Both
options.description: A kind for the definition and a record per schedule for its runtime state (paused, next firing).

questions.question: Who owns the timer: the schedule system, or a firing service in the hub?
questions.why: It decides how much the hub grows and how 'Nothing runs later by itself' stays true when the system is off.

options.label: The system owns it
options.description: The system keeps each schedule's next firing on an @ayepi/work queue in its own data folder and asks the hub to start the run as the owner (new: runs.start with an idempotency key, kindFns, chats.open, ctx.notify). The hub never needs dayspan or zones; switching the system off stops every timer; the `runs` grant is flagged on review.

options.label: A hub firing service
options.description: The system hands the hub 'run this at T as P' and the hub's durable queue holds it. Survives the system being down, but the hub grows a scheduler and every future 'later' feature lands in it.

questions.question: Who does a scheduled run run as?
questions.why: A run that starts with nobody watching acts with someone's permissions and spends someone's budget.

options.label: Its owner only
options.description: The person who made it, always. Sharing lets others see and copy it (a copy runs as them). An owner turned off or who loses access to the fn: firings are refused and recorded, and they (or admins) are told once.

options.label: Owner, and admins may schedule for a group
options.description: An admin can make a schedule that runs once for each member of a group, as them.

options.label: Everyone it is shared with
options.description: Sharing a schedule gives each person their own firings, as themselves.

sections.title: The args program
sections.intro: The args are one gin program whose result is the target fn's args; fixed args are a literal. It reads `fire` (the firing's planned instant, local time, day, time, zone, count, how late, run-now) at least.

questions.question: Besides `fire`, what can the args program read?
questions.why: More reach makes schedules more useful but blurs them into code fns and makes a firing's args harder to predict on the page.

options.label: `fire` and the previous firing's result
options.description: `previous`: the last firing that ran, its time, status and result (typed as the target's result), for 'what's new since last time'. No fn calls: a firing that needs another fn's data schedules a code fn.

options.label: Only `fire`
options.description: The simplest: args depend on the firing time alone.

options.label: `fire`, `previous`, and read-only fn calls
options.description: The program may call fns that only read (counted in the firing), like a code fn's program.

questions.question: How does the chat model write args that change with each firing?
questions.why: Gin's program schema is large and models get it wrong; the person also has to read and edit these on the page.

options.label: In plain words, written by an authoring step
options.description: `args` holds fixed JSON; `compute` holds words ('from: the firing's day minus 7 days'). A small agent on the code system's program tools writes the gin, checks it against the target's args and previews the next three firings. The words are kept for the page.

options.label: The model writes gin directly
options.description: schedule/add takes a gin expression with the typed schema, as make_code's agent does.

options.label: Fixed args only, for now
options.description: No computed args in the first build; `fire` comes later.

questions.question: Where does a firing's result go?
questions.why: This is how the person finds out what their schedule did, and where they follow up or undo it.

options.label: The schedule's own chat, plus a notification
options.description: Each schedule gets a chat (made at its first firing) where every firing is an invocation turn: run cards, follow-up questions, undo. A push when it finishes (per schedule: always, failures only, never; default always).

options.label: One 'Scheduled' chat for all, plus a notification
options.description: Every schedule's firings in one chat of the person's.

options.label: Notification and run page only
options.description: No chat; the push links to the run and the calendar shows the result.

questions.question: A firing's target asks for approval and nobody is watching. What happens?
questions.why: Writes on a schedule are the riskiest part; a firing stuck waiting forever blocks the next ones.

options.label: Wait and notify; allow at creation; admin can refuse
options.description: It waits in the owner's inbox (with the push the hub already sends) until the next firing or 24 h, then is recorded as expired. The add card offers 'Let its runs go ahead without asking' (an always-approval narrowed to this schedule's runs: policies gain `via`). An admin config can make such firings refused instead.

options.label: Wait and notify only
options.description: No allow-at-creation: each firing that needs approval waits for the person.

options.label: Always refuse
options.description: A scheduled run that needs approval is cancelled and recorded; the person sets a policy if they want it to run.

questions.question: Firings were missed (the hub or system was down). What happens when it's back?
questions.why: A daily report shouldn't run seven times after a week offline, but a 9:00 reminder missed at 8:58 should still go.

options.label: Run the latest once, if within a grace window
options.description: The most recent missed firing runs once, marked late, if it is younger than the grace window (admin config, default 6 h); the rest are recorded as missed. Per schedule it can be set to never catch up.

options.label: Never catch up
options.description: Missed firings are recorded as missed; the next on-time one runs.

options.label: Run every missed firing
options.description: Each runs in order, late.

questions.question: A firing is due while the last one still runs (a long agent, a wait for approval). Default?
questions.why: Overlapping runs of the same work can double effects or pile up spend.

options.label: Skip it
options.description: Recorded as skipped, naming the run it waited on. Per schedule it can be set to queue or replace.

options.label: Queue one
options.description: At most one waits and starts when the running one settles.

options.label: Replace the running one
options.description: The running one is cancelled and the new one starts.

questions.question: The hub's injected `limits` item says 'Nothing runs later by itself'. How does that change when the schedule system is installed, without hub text naming the system?
questions.why: A false sentence in the prompt makes the model refuse what the app can now do; hard-coding the system's name in the hub breaks the 'a system that isn't there leaves no trace' rule.

options.label: A context item can replace another
options.description: Split limits.md into `hub/limits` (accounts, setup) and `hub/later` (nothing runs later, no messages later). `InjectDecl.replaces`: while the schedule system's item is in, `hub/later` is left out (reason `replaced`, shown on the Injected tab) and the system's item says what is still true (only at times, never on events; only the person is notified). Reviewed as an `injects` change.

options.label: Admins switch it off by hand
options.description: Installing the system tells admins to switch `hub/limits` off for the chat agents; nothing automatic.

options.label: The hub item names a capability it needs to be false
options.description: `hub/later` declares it goes out when any live system holds the `runs` grant; no new field on the system's side.
